title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
statement: Given two sorted arrays a of length m and b of length n, return the median of the combined sorted sequence. The overall run time must be O(log(m + n)). Either array may be empty, but not both.
realWorld: Computing a percentile across two already-sorted shards without shipping either one across the network. A monitoring system holds latency samples sorted per region; the p50 of the union has to come out of a request that touches a logarithmic number of entries, because streaming both shards to one node is the cost you are trying to avoid. The same routine generalises to any k-th order statistic over two sorted runs.

examples.explanation: Combined length 3 is odd. The cut leaves {1,2} on the left and {3} on the right; the median is max of the left half = 2.
Combined length 4 is even, so the median averages the two elements straddling the cut: max(left) = 2 and min(right) = 3 give 2.5. Note the answer is not in either array's own middle.
The empty array is the case the sentinels exist for. i is forced to 0, so aLeft = -infinity and aRight = +infinity, and both comparisons pass immediately.

bruteForce.idea: Merge the two arrays the way merge sort's merge step does, then index the middle.

bruteForce.whySlow: You asked for one or two values and the merge produced m + n of them. Every element past the midpoint is written into the output array and never read — on two arrays of a thousand each, that is a thousand pointless copies. Worse, the merge derives the full ordering when the question only needs to know *how many* elements are below the cut, not what they are. Halving the work by stopping at the middle still leaves O(m + n); the waste is not the tail of the merge, it is that the merge walks one element at a time through two structures that each allow jumping.

patternIdentification:
The median is defined by a *cut*, not by a value: it is the place where you can split the union into a left half and a right half of (almost) equal size such that everything on the left is <= everything on the right. Because both inputs are already sorted, a cut of the union is fully described by two numbers — how many elements you take from the front of a, and how many from the front of b — and those two numbers are not independent: once you fix i, the count j is forced to be half - i. So there is only one free variable.

That free variable lives in [0, m], and the predicate 'is my cut too far left?' is monotone in it: push i right and aLeft only grows while bRight only grows, so once the cut is too far right it stays too far right. One free variable plus a monotone predicate is the signature of binary search — and note that you are searching over *positions*, not over values. Whenever the answer is characterised by a balance condition rather than by an element you could look up, ask what single parameter determines the configuration and binary search on that parameter.

optimized.idea:
Binary search the partition point of the smaller array.

Set-up. Always search the shorter array; if a is longer, swap the arguments. That keeps the search range [0, m] small and, more importantly, guarantees j = half - i never goes negative or past n.

The invariant. Let half = (m + n + 1) / 2. Choose i in [0, m] elements from the front of a and j = half - i elements from the front of b. By construction the left side always holds exactly `half` elements — the +1 makes the left side the larger one when the total is odd, which is why the odd case needs no second lookup. Name the four elements around the two cuts:

  aLeft  = a[i-1]   aRight = a[i]
  bLeft  = b[j-1]   bRight = b[j]

The cut is correct when both cross-comparisons hold: aLeft <= bRight and bLeft <= aRight. Within each array the ordering is free (a[i-1] <= a[i] because a is sorted), so those two cross-checks are the only thing that can fail, and together they mean max(left) <= min(right) — the definition of a valid split.

The sentinels. When i = 0 there is no a[i-1]; when i = m there is no a[i]. Instead of branching, set aLeft = Integer.MIN_VALUE and aRight = Integer.MAX_VALUE in those cases (and likewise for b). This is not a trick to avoid an exception — it is semantically right. 'Take nothing from a' should never be rejected for the reason 'a's left side is too big', and -infinity makes aLeft <= bRight vacuously true. Symmetrically, +infinity makes a full array never block the right side. With the sentinels, the empty-array case and the all-from-one-array case fall out of the same four lines as everything else.

Moving. If aLeft > bRight you took too much from a: the cut must move left, so high = i - 1. Otherwise bLeft > aRight, you took too little from a, and low = i + 1. Each step halves [0, m], so the loop runs O(log(min(m, n))) times, which is within O(log(m + n)).

Reading the answer. Once the cut is valid, max(aLeft, bLeft) is the largest element of the left half. If m + n is odd the left half has one extra element and that maximum *is* the median. If m + n is even the median averages it with min(aRight, bRight), the smallest element of the right half. Divide by 2.0, not 2, or you truncate.
code: public static double findMedianSortedArrays(int[] a, int[] b) {
if (a.length > b.length) return findMedianSortedArrays(b, a);   // always binary search the SHORTER array
int half = (m + n + 1) / 2;   // the +1 puts the extra element on the left when the total is odd
int j = half - i;         // the two cuts are not independent: fixing i fixes j
if (aLeft > bRight) high = i - 1;   // took too much from a
else low = i + 1;                   // took too little from a

commonMistakes: Binary searching the longer array, or forgetting the swap altogether. j = half - i then runs off the end of b: with a = [1,2,3,4,5] and b = [6], i can reach 5 while half is 3, so j = -2 and b[j] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. The sample cases with two similar-sized arrays never trigger it.

Using `half = (m + n) / 2` instead of `(m + n + 1) / 2`. Both halves are then equal when the total is even, but on an odd total the left side is the *smaller* one, so `return leftMax` returns the element just below the median — a = [1,3], b = [2] gives 1.0 instead of 2.0.

Handling the array edges with explicit if-branches instead of the ±infinity sentinels, and missing one. The usual casualty is an empty input: a = [], b = [1] leaves i = 0 with no a[i-1] to read, and the code either throws or falls through the loop and returns 0.0 — a silent wrong answer on the smallest legal input.
